job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# Drafting Problems in S. 2817 (Manager's Amendment of October 6, 2026)

I worked only from the text you provided. I could not check the official version, the amendment's status, or current law, so please verify citations against congress.gov before Thursday.

1. **Sec. 2(1)(A), volume threshold:** The 10,000-metric-ton test applies "by a single vessel" per year, so an operator could split recovery across several vessels, or stay just under the limit, and still mine commercially. The threshold also implies that sub-threshold mining is lawful, which weakens our argument that no one can mine this seabed without serious damage.

2. **Sec. 2(1):** "Commercial" is not defined. Without a revenue, sale, or intent test, operators can argue that large test or pilot collections are not "commercial."

3. **Sec. 2(1)(A):** "Recovery" and "mineral resources" are undefined, and the bill sets no measurement method (wet or dry weight, retained versus discarded sediment, or ore transferred to another ship). Tonnage is easy to dispute.

4. **Sec. 2(1)(B):** "The Secretary" is not identified. Sec. 6 refers to the Secretary of State, so readers could reasonably assume a different official. "Comparable" has no standard, procedure, notice requirement, or review standard, which invites both litigation and inconsistent use.

5. **Sec. 2(2), "U.S. person":** The definition excludes foreign-incorporated subsidiaries of U.S. companies, partnerships, trusts, and LLCs (it is unclear whether an LLC is a "corporation"). It also does not clearly cover D.C. or the territories ("State" is undefined). This undermines the "anywhere" reach in Sec. 3(a).

6. **Sec. 3(a), "person":** "Person" is undefined and would fall back on the general definition in 1 U.S.C. § 1. The bill should define it expressly, including for the entities that would actually conduct mining.

7. **Sec. 2(3), "covered vessel":** The 5,000-gross-ton threshold and the phrase "equipped for" are both open to dispute. Smaller vessels fall outside the registry, and "operator" is not defined anywhere.

8. **Sec. 3(a), "engage in":** The phrase does not clearly reach financing, insurance, equipment supply, chartering, port services, or sponsorship. Companies could structure around the ban by acting as service providers or investors.

9. **Sec. 3(a), "in the United States":** The bill does not define "United States" and does not say whether it includes the EEZ, the continental shelf, or the territories. It also does not address foreign-flagged vessels or non-U.S. entities operating beyond U.S. jurisdiction.

10. **Sec. 3(a), missing import ban:** Nothing prohibits importing, selling, or processing minerals mined abroad. Without this, the domestic ban can be circumvented through supply chains.

11. **Sec. 3(b), grandfathering:** "Exploration license" is undefined. The bill does not require that the license be active or that mining stay within its scope, and it does not address renewal, transfer, or expiration. This is one of the largest carve-out risks in the text.

12. **Sec. 3(c), "environmental assessment":** There is no cap on scale, duration, or volume and no approval, reporting, or disclosure requirement. The purpose test is subjective and hard to disprove, so commercial-scale extraction could be labeled "assessment." The term also overlaps with the NEPA term of art, which may create confusion.

13. **Sec. 4, registry and reports:** Neither registration nor quarterly reporting has a deadline, content standard, verification requirement, or public availability requirement. Sec. 5 penalizes only violations of Sec. 3, so failures to register or report carry no penalty.

14. **Sec. 5(a) and Sec. 8, date conflict:** Sec. 5(a) applies penalties to violations "on or after the date of enactment," but Sec. 8 delays the Act's effect by 180 days. The bill should state which date governs the prohibition and the penalties.

15. **Sec. 5(a), enforcement:** The bill names no enforcing agency and includes no citizen-suit provision, injunctive authority, or forfeiture of vessels, equipment, minerals, or profits. A $1 million daily penalty may be small relative to project revenue. It is also unclear whether a continuing operation counts as one violation or one per day.

16. **Sec. 5(b), "willfully":** "Willfully" is undefined, and the bill does not address corporate officers or aiding-and-abetting liability.

17. **Sec. 6:** "Shall seek to negotiate" creates no enforceable obligation. There is no reporting to Congress, no consequence for failure, and "equivalent" is undefined. The section also does not address coordination with the International Seabed Authority.

18. **Sec. 7(a) versus Sec. 7(b), direct conflict:** Sec. 7(a) keeps the prohibition in effect indefinitely until a joint resolution finds mining safe, but Sec. 7(b) ends the entire Act after 10 years. As drafted, the ban lapses automatically regardless of findings. This is the most important fix, because it contradicts our goal of a permanent prohibition.

19. **Sec. 7(a), trigger and repeal path:** "Serious harm" is undefined. The bill sets no deadline or mechanism for the National Academies report, and it does not say what expedited procedures apply to the joint resolution. A simple-majority joint resolution could repeal the ban, so the threshold for lifting it should be stated clearly.

20. **Sec. 8, 180-day gap:** During the 180 days between enactment and the effective date, companies could accelerate activity, and the bill is unclear about whether mining in that window is unlawful. Combined with Sec. 3(b), this creates a window for licenses or operations to be expanded before the ban takes effect.

21. **Missing severability clause:** If a court strikes Sec. 2(1)(B) or the U.S. person definition, the Act could collapse entirely or leave gaps that companies could exploit. A severability clause is standard and should be added.

22. **Missing relationship to existing law and rulemaking:** The bill does not state whether it supersedes or preempts existing deep-seabed licensing under the Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act (30 U.S.C. § 1401 et seq.). It also grants no rulemaking authority and no appropriations for NOAA's new registry and enforcement duties. Staff should verify the DSHMRA interaction, since I cannot confirm the current statute.

**Priority fixes before Thursday:**

- Resolve the Sec. 7(a)/(b) conflict so the prohibition has no automatic sunset.
- Narrow the Sec. 3(b) exploration-license grandfather and Sec. 3(c) assessment carve-out.
- Add an import, sale, and processing ban, and fix the "U.S. person" and "engage in" definitions.
- Reconcile the Sec. 5 and Sec. 8 effective dates.
- Give the registry and reports a penalty and an enforcing agency.

I can draft proposed replacement language for any of these items.
